To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) HIV‐1‐ infected CD4+ cells are susceptible to lysis by non‐adherent peripheral mononuclear cells; 2) the lysis is mediated by NK cells; 3) lysis of HIV1‐infected Sup‐1 cells does not require the presence of interferon alpha (IFN‐ alpha)‐producing cells; 4) lysis of A. 25‐sup‐1 cells requires the presence of IFN‐alpha producing
HIV‐1‐ infected cells are susceptible to natural killer cell‐mediation lysis and that interferon‐alpha production is required for the NK cell lysis of HIV1‐infected cells.
NK cells can kill HIV‐1‐positive T cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which NK cells recognize and kill HIV‐1‐ infected T cells.
the study of the mechanisms involved in the pathogenicity of HIV.
the role of NK cells in the immune response to HIV-1 infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV infection of T cells is not a target for NK cell‐lysis.
NK cell lysis of HIV-1 infected cells is dependent on the type of virus and the type of cell infected, and is not dependent on the presence of IFN-alpha.
NK cells are capable of lysing HIV‐1 infected CD4+ T cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NK cells may be able to recognize HIV‐1 infected cells in the absence of IFN‐α, but that IFN‐α may be required for optimal lysis.
HIV‐1‐induced T cell death may be due to a combination of mechanisms.
NK cells are not the major effector cells in HIV‐1 disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NK cells are capable of killing HIV‐infected T cells.
HIV‐1‐specific CD8+ T cells can be activated to kill HIV‐1‐expressing cells in the presence of IL‐12.
NK cell lysis of infected T cells is not a universal phenomenon.
